messages.content: How do I ask "Can you help me?" in French? I need it for my boss and for a friend, and I gather they're not the same.

They differ by exactly one word — the "you":

- To your friend: **Tu peux m'aider ?**
- To your boss: **Vous pouvez m'aider ?**

French has two words for "you": *tu* for one person you know well (friends, family, children, fellow students) and *vous* for politeness — a boss, an older person, a stranger, an official. The verb changes shape with it: *pouvoir* (to be able) gives *tu peux* but *vous pouvez*. There is no way to dodge the choice; every "you" sentence forces it.

The little *m'* is "me", tucked in front of the verb: *m'aider* = "to help me". And the matching "please" changes too: *s'il te plaît* with tu, *s'il vous plaît* with vous. When in doubt with anyone you don't know, start with vous — nobody is ever offended by being given the respectful form.
I'm writing two emails in French: one to a clerk at the préfecture, one to my colleague Claire. How do the opening and closing change?

Almost everything in the frame flips, because the préfecture gets *vous* and Claire gets *tu*.

**To the clerk (vous, formal):**
- Opening: *Madame, Monsieur,* (no name needed for an office)
- A typical line: *Je vous écris pour demander un rendez-vous.* ("I'm writing to ask for an appointment" — *vous* is the formal "you")
- Closing: *Cordialement,* for normal business politeness. The full ceremonial version, *Veuillez agréer, Madame, Monsieur, l'expression de mes salutations distinguées*, still exists for administration, but it is very heavy — save it for formal letters, not email.

**To Claire (tu, friendly):**
- Opening: *Bonjour Claire,*
- Same sentence, informal: *Je t'écris pour te demander un truc.* 
- Closing: *Merci !* or *À bientôt,*

Notice the machinery: *je vous écris / je t'écris*, *votre dossier / ton dossier*. Every "you" and "your" in the email has two forms, and staying in one register from greeting to signature is what makes the email sound right.
"Tell me" — my phrasebook gives both "dis-moi" and "dites-moi". Which is which, and why does the verb look different?

Both are "tell me" — *dis-moi* is the tu command, *dites-moi* the vous command, from the verb *dire* (to say/tell).

Commands in French glue the pronoun onto the end of the verb with a hyphen, and *me* becomes *moi* in that position: *dis* + *moi*, *dites* + *moi*. The verb stem itself follows the register: *dis* is the tu form, *dites* the vous form.

The pattern repeats everywhere:

- *Regarde-moi !* / *Regardez-moi !* — look at me
- *Écoute-moi !* / *Écoutez-moi !* — listen to me
- *Assieds-toi !* / *Asseyez-vous !* — sit down (note *toi* and *vous* doing the same job as *moi*)
- *Dépêche-toi !* / *Dépêchez-vous !* — hurry up

So when you hear a command ending in *-ez* plus a hyphenated pronoun, it's vous; the shorter stem plus *-moi/-toi* is tu.
Give me a side-by-side reference of everyday French phrases in tu form vs vous form.

Everyday phrases, tu vs vous:

| Meaning | Tu (one friend) | Vous (formal / plural) |
|---|---|---|
| you speak | tu parles | vous parlez |
| you want | tu veux | vous voulez |
| you can | tu peux | vous pouvez |
| you have | tu as | vous avez |
| you are | tu es | vous êtes |
| your name | ton nom | votre nom |
| your house | ta maison | votre maison |
| tell me | dis-moi | dites-moi |
| excuse me | excuse-moi | excusez-moi |
| come here | viens | venez |
| wait | attends | attendez |
| please | s'il te plaît | s'il vous plaît |

Two patterns worth noticing. First, the vous verb forms mostly end in *-ez* (parlez, voulez, pouvez, venez) — but three very common verbs break the rule: *vous êtes* (être), *vous faites* (faire), *vous dites* (dire). Learn those three as exceptions. Second, vous does double duty: it is also the only way to say "you" to more than one person, even close friends together.
I said "Vous venez demain ?" to two of my friends at once and my teacher said it was right — but I thought vous was the formal one?

Your teacher is right, and you've found the second job of *vous*: it is also the plural "you", for any group, however close.

*Tu* is strictly one person. The moment you address two or more people — two best friends, your parents, a room full of children — the word is *vous* and the verb follows: *Vous venez demain, les amis ?* ("Are you [both/all] coming tomorrow, guys?"). Nobody hears formality in it; context makes it obvious you're being plural, not polite.

So *vous* means one of two things: one person at respectful distance, or several people at any distance. French has no separate word for the plural, the way English once had "ye". When you want to underline the group, you can add a word: *Vous deux, vous venez ?* ("You two — are you coming?")
Je viens d'arriver dans mon immeuble à Lyon. Avec ma voisine, une dame de soixante-dix ans, je dis tu ou vous ? Et avec le gardien, qui a mon âge ?

Avec votre voisine de soixante-dix ans : **vous**, sans hésitation. Dites « Bonjour Madame, vous allez bien ? » L'âge et la politesse demandent *vous* au début d'une relation. Si un jour elle vous propose « On peut se tutoyer ? », vous pourrez changer — mais c'est à elle de le proposer.

Avec le gardien, qui a votre âge : *vous* aussi pour le premier contact, par prudence. Ensuite, entre voisins du même âge, le *tu* vient souvent naturellement. Après quelques conversations, vous pouvez proposer : « On se tutoie ? »

La règle simple : commencez toujours par *vous* avec un adulte que vous ne connaissez pas. Il est facile de passer de *vous* à *tu* quand la relation devient amicale ; l'inverse est presque impossible.
"What's your name?" — I've seen "Comment tu t'appelles ?" and "Comment vous appelez-vous ?" Are both right?

Both are right — they're the tu and vous versions of the same question, from the verb *s'appeler* (to be called, literally "to call oneself").

- To a child, a student, a new friend: **Comment tu t'appelles ?**
- To an adult you've just met formally: **Comment vous appelez-vous ?**

Notice the machinery differs. In the tu version the little reflexive word sits before the verb: *tu t'appelles* ("you call yourself"). In the vous version the pronoun flips behind the verb with a hyphen — that's inversion, the formal question style: *vous appelez-vous*.

The answer is the same for everyone: *Je m'appelle...* And to hand the question back: *Et toi ?* (tu) or *Et vous ?* (vous).
Why do some vous forms look nothing like the tu forms? Tu es but vous êtes, tu fais but vous faites...

Most vous forms are built regularly with *-ez*: *vous parlez, vous voulez, vous pouvez, vous venez, vous allez*. But a tiny club of extremely common verbs keeps old, irregular vous forms that you simply have to memorize:

- être (to be): tu es → **vous êtes**
- faire (to do/make): tu fais → **vous faites**
- dire (to say): tu dis → **vous dites**

These three — *êtes, faites, dites* — are the complete rebel set among common verbs, and they are worth learning as a trio because you will use them constantly: *Vous êtes prêt ?* (Are you ready?), *Qu'est-ce que vous faites ?* (What are you doing?), *Vous dites... ?* (You're saying...?).

The pattern behind it: the most frequent words in a language resist regularization, because everyone hears them too often for the "wrong" form to be smoothed away. English does the same thing — "you are", never "you be" in standard speech, and "I am / you are / he is" all from different roots.
How do I ask a stranger where the station is, versus asking my friend? I want both versions, word for word.

To a stranger, wrap it in politeness and vous:

**Pardon, Madame — vous savez où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ?**
("Excuse me, madam — do you know where the station is, please?")

Even softer, the full classic opener: *Excusez-moi de vous déranger, où est la gare, s'il vous plaît ?* ("Sorry to bother you...")

To your friend, everything relaxes into tu and the politeness wrapping falls away:

**Tu sais où est la gare, toi ?** — or even shorter, the way friends actually talk: **La gare, c'est où ?**

Notice what does *not* change: *où est la gare* is identical in both. The only moving parts are the "you" machinery — *vous savez / tu sais*, *s'il vous plaît / s'il te plaît* — and the apology opener, which a friend doesn't need.
Halfway through a conversation with my landlady I realized I'd been switching between tu and vous. Why did it sound so strange, and how do I fix it mid-conversation?

It sounded strange because tu and vous aren't just grammar — they're a running signal of how you define the relationship. *Vous* says "respectful distance"; *tu* says "we're close". Switching back and forth sounds like you keep re-deciding who she is, sentence by sentence. French even has verbs for the act itself: *tutoyer* (to address someone as tu) and *vouvoyer* (to address someone as vous).

A landlady is vous territory. The fix is painless:

1. Settle on **vous** and stay there.
2. If you want to acknowledge the wobble, one light *Pardonnez-moi* is enough — you don't need to explain a grammar slip.
3. Keep every "you" and "your" in the same register afterwards: *vous, votre, chez vous*.

The standing rule that prevents this: when you're unsure, choose vous and hold it. Nobody is offended by too much respect, and the other person can always offer *Tu peux me tutoyer* ("You can use tu with me") — an invitation that only ever travels in that direction.
My French colleague wrote "Je suis actuellement en réunion." I read it as "I am actually in a meeting" — is that right?

Not quite — you've met one of the classic false friends. *Actuellement* means **currently, at the moment**, not "actually":

**Je suis actuellement en réunion.** = "I'm in a meeting right now."

"Actually" in the English sense (in fact, really) is *en fait* or *en réalité*:

- **Actuellement, il pleut.** — It's raining at the moment.
- **En fait, il ne pleut pas.** — Actually, it isn't raining.

A reliable check: if you can replace "actually" with "currently" and the English still works, French wants *actuellement*. If it means "in fact / contrary to what you'd think", it's *en fait*.
A form says the decision will arrive "éventuellement dans un mois." Does that mean it will definitely come within a month, eventually?

No — and this one matters, because the French is making much less of a promise than the English suggests. *Éventuellement* means **possibly, maybe, if circumstances allow**:

**Éventuellement dans un mois.** = "Possibly within a month." No commitment at all.

"Eventually" in English (in the end, sooner or later, it will happen) is *finalement* or *à la longue*:

- **La décision arrivera finalement.** — The decision will eventually arrive. (It will come, in the end.)
- **La décision arrivera éventuellement.** — The decision might arrive. (Or might not.)

The same trap lives in the adjective: *un éventuel retard* is "a possible delay", not "an eventual delay". Whenever you see *éventuel-* in an official document, translate it as "possible" and you'll never over-read a promise again.
I told my host family "Je vais assister ma voisine avec ses courses" meaning I'd help her with her shopping. They smiled. What did I say?

You said you'd *attend* your neighbor, like an event. *Assister à* means **to be present at, to attend**:

- **J'ai assisté à un concert.** — I attended a concert.
- **Elle assiste à une réunion.** — She's attending a meeting.

To help someone is *aider*: **Je vais aider ma voisine à faire ses courses.** Note the construction — *aider quelqu'un à faire quelque chose*: you help a person (directly, no preposition) *à* do the thing.

The pair is worth fixing side by side in memory, because the two verbs swap jobs between the languages: French *assister à* = English "attend"; French *aider* = English "assist/help". Your sentence mixed the French verb with the English meaning — the most common kind of false-friend error, and an easy one to smile at.
What's the difference between attendre and assister? I keep using attendre for "attend a class."

The two verbs point in opposite directions:

**Attendre** = to wait (for). It already contains the "for", so it takes its object directly, with no preposition:
- **J'attends le bus depuis dix minutes.** — I've been waiting for the bus for ten minutes.
- **Attends-moi !** — Wait for me!

**Assister à** = to attend, to be present at:
- **J'assiste à un cours de français le mardi.** — I attend a French class on Tuesdays.
- **Nous avons assisté au mariage.** — We attended the wedding.

So your sentence for class should be *j'assiste à un cours*. The clean contrast: *J'attends mon professeur* = "I'm waiting for my teacher (he's late)"; *J'assiste à son cours* = "I attend his class (I'm in the room, learning)". English "attend" and French *attendre* look identical and do completely different jobs — that's exactly what makes it a false friend.
Where do I go in Paris to borrow books, and where to buy them? I keep mixing up librairie and bibliothèque.

Buy them at the **librairie**, borrow them at the **bibliothèque**:

- **Je vais à la librairie acheter un roman.** — I'm going to the bookshop to buy a novel.
- **J'étudie à la bibliothèque le soir.** — I study at the library in the evening.

A *librairie* is a shop: it sells books, and the *libraire* is the bookseller. A *bibliothèque* is the lending library, with cards, desks and silence. English "library" maps onto *bibliothèque*, never onto *librairie*.

Memory hook: a *librairie* is where the *livres* have price tags. If money changes hands, it's the librairie.
My friend said "Quelle déception !" after the match. Was she saying the team deceived her?

No — she was saying they let her down. *Une déception* is **a disappointment**, and *décevoir* is "to disappoint":

- **Quelle déception !** — What a letdown!
- **Le film m'a déçu.** — The film disappointed me.

"Deception" — deliberately misleading someone — is *la tromperie*, from the verb *tromper*:

- **La publicité nous a trompés.** — The advertising deceived/misled us.
- **Il m'a trompé.** — He deceived me (or cheated on me, in a relationship context).

So the emotional split is: *déception* is what you feel when reality falls short; *tromperie* is what someone does to you on purpose. Your friend's team didn't lie to her — they just played badly, which in football can feel worse.
After lunch I said "Je vais rester" because I wanted a rest. My host looked confused — why?

Because *rester* means **to stay, to remain** — so you announced "I'm going to stay", and your host was waiting to hear stay *where*, or stay *how long*.

To rest is *se reposer*:

- **Je suis fatigué, je vais me reposer.** — I'm tired, I'm going to rest.
- **Je reste à la maison ce soir.** — I'm staying home tonight. (rester, used correctly)

*Rester* also handles "left/remaining", which will help you recognize it: **Il reste du pain** = "There's some bread left." Same verb — what remains, stays.

So: staying somewhere → *rester*; resting your body → *se reposer*. English "rest" and French *rester* share Latin ancestry, which is exactly why they trick you.
I read "Il s'est blessé au genou" in a match report. Blesser looks like "bless" — that can't be right?

Your instinct is correct — it's a false friend. *Blesser* means **to wound, to hurt, to injure**:

- **Il s'est blessé au genou.** — He injured his knee. (The reflexive *se blesser* = to hurt oneself.)
- **Une blessure** is a wound or an injury — the word you'll see in every sports report.

It also works for feelings: **Tes mots m'ont blessé** = "Your words hurt me."

To bless, in the religious sense, is *bénir*: **Le prêtre a béni les enfants.** — The priest blessed the children.

So the pair: *blesser* = hurt (body or feelings), *bénir* = bless. A player who is *blessé* is going off on a stretcher, not receiving a blessing — though at that point he might want both.
Ma correspondante m'a écrit « Bonne journée ! » à la fin de son mail. C'est comme « bon voyage » ?

Non, ce n'est pas la même chose — et c'est un faux ami classique.

**Journée** veut dire le jour comme durée, le jour vécu : « Bonne journée ! » signifie « passe une bonne journée », comme "have a nice day" en anglais. On le dit le matin ou au début de la journée.

**Voyage**, c'est le déplacement, le trajet loin de chez soi : « Bon voyage ! » se dit à quelqu'un qui part loin.

Deux exemples pour fixer la différence :
- **Je travaille toute la journée.** — Je travaille pendant tout le jour.
- **Je pars en voyage demain.** — Je pars loin, en déplacement.

Petit détail utile : *le jour* compte les jours (trois jours, le jour de mon départ), et *la journée* raconte le jour comme une expérience (une longue journée, une belle journée).
Give me a reference table of the classic French false friends — the word, what it looks like it means, what it really means, and the French word for the English meaning.

Classic French false friends:

| French word | Looks like | Really means | For the English word, use |
|---|---|---|---|
| actuellement | actually | currently, at present | en fait |
| éventuellement | eventually | possibly, maybe | finalement |
| assister à | to assist | to attend, be present at | aider |
| attendre | to attend | to wait (for) | assister à |
| librairie | library | bookshop | bibliothèque |
| déception | deception | disappointment | tromperie |
| rester | to rest | to stay, remain | se reposer |
| blesser | to bless | to hurt, wound | bénir |
| une journée | a journey | a day (as lived duration) | un voyage |
| sensible | sensible | sensitive | raisonnable |

How to use the table: the danger is never in reading these words in a list — it's in mid-sentence, when your brain grabs the English twin and runs. The two that cause real-world misunderstandings are *éventuellement* (a "maybe" read as a promise) and *actuellement* (a "right now" read as "in fact"). If you fix only those two, you'll have defused the worst of the set.
How am I supposed to know if a French noun is le or la? Are there any patterns that actually help?

There are patterns — they give you good odds, never certainty. The most useful ones:

**Usually feminine:** endings in *-tion / -sion* (la nation, la décision), *-té* (la liberté, la santé), *-ette* (la fourchette).

**Usually masculine:** endings in *-age* (le garage, le fromage, le voyage), *-ment* (le gouvernement, le moment), *-eau* (le bateau, le cadeau).

Now the honest part: the exceptions are common words. *La plage* and *l'image* break the *-age* rule; *la maison* is feminine despite its ending. So treat the patterns as a first guess for new words, not a law.

The method that actually works: never learn a noun naked. Learn *la table*, *le livre*, *la plage* — article welded on, as one vocabulary item. Then agreement later (grande table, bon livre) has something solid to copy.
Why is it "le problème" if words ending in -e are usually feminine? And "la main" looks masculine to me.

*Le problème* belongs to a family with a passport from Greek. Words that came from Greek neuter nouns ending in *-ma* entered French (and Spanish — compare *el problema*) as **masculine**, whatever their final letter looks like:

- **le problème, le système, le thème, le poème, le programme, le diplôme**

So the rule isn't "ending in -e = feminine" failing; it's an older rule winning. If a word ends in *-ème, -gramme, -ome* and feels abstract or technical, bet masculine.

*La main* (the hand) is the opposite kind of rebel: an old feminine noun that kept its gender even though *-ain* usually signals masculine (compare *le pain*, *le train*). There's no deeper logic to find — it has simply always been *la main*.

Practical takeaway: learn both as vocabulary with their articles attached — *le problème*, *la main* — and let the two famous rebels remind you that gender is a property of the word, not a conclusion you draw from its spelling.
J'ai écrit « une grand maison avec un bonne jardin » et mon prof a corrigé deux mots. Pourquoi ?

Parce que l'adjectif copie le genre du nom qu'il décrit — et vos deux erreurs vont dans des directions opposées.

1. **Maison** est féminin, donc *grand* devient **grande** : « une **grande** maison ».
2. **Jardin** est masculin, donc *bonne* redevient **bon** : « un **bon** jardin ».

La phrase corrigée : « Une grande maison avec un bon jardin. »

Retenez les paires complètes, comme des unités :
- un grand jardin / une grande maison
- un bon café / une bonne soupe
- un petit appartement / une petite rue

Le réflexe à développer : avant d'écrire l'adjectif, trouvez le nom et demandez « masculin ou féminin ? » — puis habillez l'adjectif en conséquence. En français, l'adjectif ne voyage jamais seul : il porte toujours les couleurs de son nom.
Why do I see both "beau" and "bel" for beautiful? And where does the adjective go — I thought French adjectives come after the noun.

Two separate things are going on.

**Position:** most adjectives do follow the noun (*une maison moderne, un livre intéressant*), but a small club of very common ones comes **before** it: *beau, bon, mauvais, grand, petit, jeune, vieux, nouveau, joli*. You already use two of them: *un bon café, une grande maison*.

**The three shapes of beau:** because it sits before the noun, it needs a special form in front of a vowel sound:

- **un beau jardin** — a beautiful garden (masculine, consonant)
- **un bel appartement** — a beautiful apartment (masculine, vowel: *bel*)
- **une belle maison** — a beautiful house (feminine: *belle*)

Two other adjectives follow exactly the same pattern: *nouveau / nouvel / nouvelle* (un nouvel an — a new year) and *vieux / vieil / vieille* (un vieil ami — an old friend). Learn the trio as a set; they're the only common ones that do this.
How do plurals work for adjectives? I wrote "les robes blanc" and "les murs blanches" and both were marked wrong — in opposite directions, apparently.

Exactly opposite, yes — you gave each adjective the other one's ending. The corrected pair:

- **les robes blanches** — robes are feminine plural, so *blanc* must become *blanches*
- **les murs blancs** — murs are masculine plural, so *blanc* just adds an s: *blancs*

The system: first find the feminine singular, then pluralize it. *Blanc* is irregular: masculine *blanc*, feminine *blanche* (the c turns into ch). Then plurals are regular: *blancs / blanches*.

For most adjectives the machinery is simpler:

- grand → grands (m.pl.) / grandes (f.pl.)
- petit → petits / petites
- long → longs / longues (as in *les longues journées*)

And one merciful group: adjectives already ending in *-e* don't change for gender at all, only for number — *un livre rouge, une robe rouge, des robes rouges*. When in doubt, the checking question is always the same: what is the noun's gender and number? The adjective is just a copy.
In "elle est allée" and "elles sont venues", why does the participle keep changing? My book says the passé composé doesn't agree.

Your book gave you the avoir half of the rule. Here is the whole system:

**With être verbs, the participle agrees with the subject**, exactly like an adjective:
- il est allé / elle est allée / ils sont allés / elles sont allées
- il est venu / elle est venue / elles sont venues

**With avoir verbs, the participle does not change for the subject:**
- elle a vu le film — *vu* stays *vu*
- elles ont mangé — *mangé* stays *mangé*

So it's not that "the passé composé doesn't agree"; it's that agreement happens with *être* and not (for subjects) with *avoir*. This is why the être family — aller, venir, partir, arriver, rester and their relatives — needs the extra attention: every time you use one, the participle has to be dressed for its subject, gender and number included.
My teacher says "son" can mean his OR her. How does anyone know whose car "sa voiture" is?

Because French possessives agree with the **thing owned**, not with the owner — the exact reverse of English.

- **sa voiture** = his car *or* her car (voiture is feminine, so *sa* — the owner could be anyone)
- **son frère** = his brother *or* her brother (frère is masculine, so *son*)
- **ses enfants** = his / her / their children

So *Paul parle de sa sœur* uses *sa* because *sœur* is feminine — even though Paul is a man. English asks "who owns it?"; French asks "what is owned, and what's its gender?"

In practice, context almost always settles whose car it is. When it genuinely doesn't, French clarifies with a name: *la voiture de Marie*, or *son frère à lui* ("his brother — his, that guy's"). Once you stop expecting *son/sa* to tell you the owner's gender, the ambiguity stops bothering you — French speakers simply don't look for that information there.
Peux-tu corriger ce petit texte ? « Le maison de mon amie est grand. Elle a un jardin avec des fleurs rouge et un chat noir très belle. »

Bien sûr. Voici le texte corrigé :

« **La** maison de mon amie est **grande**. Elle a un jardin avec des fleurs **rouges** et un chat noir très **beau**. »

Les quatre corrections, une par une :

1. **Le maison → La maison** : *maison* est féminin, donc l'article est *la*.
2. **grand → grande** : l'adjectif s'accorde avec *maison*, féminin singulier.
3. **rouge → rouges** : *fleurs* est féminin pluriel, donc *rouge* prend un s (rouge ne change pas pour le genre, seulement pour le nombre).
4. **belle → beau** : *chat* est masculin, donc *beau* — *belle* est la forme féminine (*une belle maison*).

La méthode de vérification : soulignez chaque nom, notez son genre et son nombre, puis vérifiez que chaque article et chaque adjectif portent les mêmes marques. En français, l'accord n'est pas une décoration — c'est la grammaire qui montre quels mots vont ensemble.
Why is it "il est français" but "elle est française"? And does the pronunciation change too?

Nationality adjectives agree like every other adjective: **français / française, américain / américaine, anglais / anglaise, allemand / allemande**. (Note the lowercase — French doesn't capitalize nationality adjectives.)

And yes, the pronunciation changes, in a very French way: the feminine form **wakes up the final consonant**.

- *il est français* — the final s is silent: roughly "fran-SAY"
- *elle est française* — the s is now pronounced, as a z sound: "fran-SAYZ"

Same with *anglais / anglaise*. The spelling logic: the masculine form ends in a consonant that is written but asleep; adding the feminine *-e* puts a vowel after it, and the consonant wakes. You'll hear this same waking effect in *grand/grande* (the d) and *bon/bonne* (the n).

So when you say *elle est française*, the little z sound at the end isn't an extra — it's the feminine marker doing its job out loud.

Here's my paragraph: "La ville est petit et propre. Les rues sont large et les maisons sont blanc. Mon hôtel est confortable et le personnel est gentille." Can you fix the agreements and tell me how to check them myself?

Corrected paragraph:

**La ville est petite et propre. Les rues sont larges et les maisons sont blanches. Mon hôtel est confortable et le personnel est gentil.**

What changed, and why:

- **ville** (f.) → *petite*. *Propre* was already fine — adjectives ending in *-e* use the same form for masculine and feminine.
- **rues** (f. pl.) → *larges*: feminine, and plural, so both marks.
- **maisons** (f. pl.) → *blanches*: remember *blanc* has the irregular feminine *blanche*.
- **personnel** → *gentil*, not *gentille*. This is the sneaky one: *le personnel* (the staff) is a masculine singular collective noun, even though it describes many people of all genders.
- **confortable** needed nothing — another *-e* adjective.

The self-checking routine: (1) underline every noun; (2) write its gender and number above it; (3) walk through the sentence and dress every article, adjective and *être*-participle to match its noun. Three of your four errors were plain gender/number copies — the routine catches all of those mechanically. The fourth, *personnel*, is a vocabulary fact: some nouns' genders simply have to be learned with the word.
I keep reading that the passé composé is for completed actions and the imparfait for background. What does that actually mean in a sentence?

Think of it as film versus snapshot.

The **imparfait** is the film running in the background — states, habits, scenes, things that were simply "on", with no edges:

- **Quand j'étais enfant, je jouais dehors tous les jours.** — When I was a child, I played outside every day. (A whole era, not one event.)
- **Il pleuvait et il faisait froid.** — It was raining and it was cold. (The weather around everything else.)

The **passé composé** is the snapshot — an event with a beginning and an end, something you could put on a timeline:

- **Hier, j'ai fini le rapport à six heures.** — Yesterday I finished the report at six o'clock. (Done. Clockable.)

The two work together in the classic combination: **Je lisais quand tu as téléphoné.** — "I was reading (film running) when you phoned (snapshot event)." Most real storytelling in the past is exactly this braid: imparfait lays down what was going on, passé composé drops in what happened.
How do I form the passé composé for regular verbs like regarder, manger, écouter?

Two pieces: the present tense of **avoir**, plus a past participle. For regular *-er* verbs, the participle is the infinitive with *-é* instead of *-er*:

- regarder → **regardé** : *j'ai regardé, tu as regardé, elle a regardé*
- manger → **mangé** : *nous avons mangé, vous avez mangé*
- écouter → **écouté** : *ils ont écouté*

In sentences: **Hier soir, nous avons regardé un film et écouté de la musique.** — Last night we watched a film and listened to music.

One listening note that surprises learners: *regardé* is pronounced exactly like *regarder* ("ruh-gar-DAY"). In speech you often can't hear the difference between "I watch" and "I watched" for these verbs — the *ai / as / a* of avoir in front is what carries the past. That's normal; context and the auxiliary do the work.
Which verbs use être instead of avoir in the passé composé? I keep saying "j'ai allé".

*J'ai allé* is the classic error — *aller* never takes avoir. A family of movement and change-of-state verbs builds the passé composé with **être** instead:

- **aller** → je suis **allé** (to go)
- **venir** → je suis **venu** (to come)
- **partir** → elle est **partie** (to leave)
- **arriver** → nous sommes **arrivés** (to arrive)
- **rester** → ils sont **restés** (to stay)
- also: entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, retourner, tomber — and naître (to be born) and mourir (to die)

Two consequences to hold onto. First, the participle **agrees with the subject**, like an adjective: *il est allé / elle est allée / elles sont allées*. Second, the list is small and closed — it's essentially verbs of coming, going and staying. Everything else defaults to avoir.

So: *Je suis allé au marché hier.* Never *j'ai allé*.
How do the two past tenses work together in a story? Like "I was walking when I saw him"?

That sentence is the textbook braid:

**Je marchais dans la rue quand j'ai vu Paul.**
The imparfait (*je marchais*) lays down the ongoing track — walking, in progress, no edges. The passé composé (*j'ai vu*) drops the event onto it — the moment of seeing, complete.

Two more of the same shape:

- **Nous dînions quand le téléphone a sonné.** — We were having dinner when the phone rang.
- **Elle lisait tranquillement quand, soudain, la porte s'est ouverte.** — She was reading quietly when, suddenly, the door opened.

Notice *soudain* (suddenly) — it's the classic signal that an event is about to interrupt the scene, and the verb after it goes in the passé composé. When you write a story, ask of each verb: is this the scenery, or is this something that *happens*? Scenery → imparfait. Happening → passé composé.
We went to the sea every summer when I was a kid, but last summer we went to Nice once. Same verb — different tense?

Yes, and your two sentences are the perfect minimal pair:

Habit, repeated every year → **imparfait**:
**Chaque été, nous allions à la mer.** — Every summer, we went (used to go) to the sea.

One single, bounded trip → **passé composé**:
**L'été dernier, nous sommes allés à Nice.** — Last summer, we went to Nice.

The signal words do most of the choosing for you. Pulling toward imparfait: *chaque été, tous les jours, toujours, souvent, d'habitude* (usually). Pulling toward passé composé: *hier, l'été dernier, une fois, soudain, d'abord... ensuite*.

A useful test: can you count it or date it? "Last summer, once, on the 14th" — passé composé. Does it describe how life generally was? — imparfait.
I'm writing about a picnic that got rained on. How do I set the scene and then make the rain arrive?

Scene first, in the imparfait — weather, activities, atmosphere, everything that was simply "on":

**Il faisait beau, les enfants jouaient dans le jardin et nous préparions le pique-nique.**
(It was fine weather, the children were playing in the garden and we were preparing the picnic.)

Then the change of state arrives in the passé composé:

**Soudain, le ciel est devenu gris et il a commencé à pleuvoir.**
(Suddenly, the sky turned grey and it started to rain.)

Details worth noticing: weather conditions live in the imparfait (*il faisait beau* — that's just how it was), while *devenir* is an être verb (*le ciel **est devenu** gris*), and *il a commencé à pleuvoir* uses *commencer à* + infinitive for the moment something starts. Scene in imparfait, plot twist in passé composé — your picnic now reads like a story instead of a list.
The participles eu, vu, pris, fait — where do they come from? They don't look like their verbs at all.

They're the irregular past participles of the most frequent avoir verbs — the ones you'll use constantly in the past tense, which is exactly why they never got regularized:

- avoir → **eu** : *j'ai eu* (I had / got)
- voir → **vu** : *j'ai vu* (I saw)
- prendre → **pris** : *j'ai pris* (I took)
- faire → **fait** : *j'ai fait* (I did / made)
- lire → **lu** : *j'ai lu* (I read)
- écrire → **écrit** : *j'ai écrit* (I wrote)
- boire → **bu** : *j'ai bu* (I drank)
- ouvrir → **ouvert** : *j'ai ouvert* (I opened)

There's no rule to derive them — learn each as a pair, verb + participle, the way you learn *le/la* with a noun. The good news: this short list covers a huge share of real past-tense speech. *Qu'est-ce que tu as fait hier ? — J'ai pris le train, j'ai lu un livre, j'ai vu un ami.* (What did you do yesterday? — I took the train, I read a book, I saw a friend.)

Je raconte mon week-end : « Samedi, je me promenais au marché quand soudain j'ai vu un vieil ami. Nous avons parlé, puis nous allions prendre un café ensemble. » Mon prof dit qu'il y a une erreur de temps à la fin. Où ?

Votre professeur a raison, et l'erreur est à la fin : **« nous allions prendre un café »** doit être au passé composé — **« puis nous sommes allés prendre un café ensemble »**.

Le reste de votre texte est correct, et il montre le bon contraste :
- *je me promenais* (imparfait) pose le décor : une action en cours, sans limites précises ;
- *j'ai vu* (passé composé) fait arriver l'événement ;
- *nous avons parlé* (passé composé) continue l'histoire.

Mais *allions* est un imparfait : il suggère un fond ou une habitude, pas l'action suivante de l'histoire. Or, aller prendre le café est exactement cela — l'étape suivante, après la conversation.

Le test à appliquer : demandez-vous « est-ce que l'histoire avance ? » Si oui, passé composé. Si le verbe décrit seulement le décor autour de l'histoire, imparfait.
In questions, how do I choose? "Qu'est-ce que tu as fait hier soir ?" versus "Qu'est-ce que tu faisais quand je t'ai appelé ?" — both are about the past.

Ask what kind of answer the question is fishing for.

**Qu'est-ce que tu as fait hier soir ?** treats last night as a closed box and asks for the completed contents — so passé composé. Natural answer: *J'ai dîné chez Léa, puis j'ai regardé un film.* (A list of finished events.)

**Qu'est-ce que tu faisais quand je t'ai appelé ?** asks what was *in progress* at one moment — so imparfait. Natural answer: *Je dormais.* (I was asleep.)

And notice the second question is itself a braid: *tu faisais* (the scene) interrupted by *je t'ai appelé* (the event, passé composé). The caller doesn't ask "what did you complete?" but "what was going on when the phone rang?"

Timeline test: if you can give the action a start and a finish, passé composé. If it was simply "on" at the moment in question, imparfait.
Give me a reference of signal words for choosing between the imparfait and the passé composé, with an example for each.

Signal words for the two past tenses:

**Imparfait — habits, background, "how things were"**

| Signal | Example |
|---|---|
| chaque jour / chaque été | Chaque été, nous allions à la mer. |
| toujours | Il lisait toujours le journal le matin. |
| souvent | Nous allions souvent au cinéma. |
| d'habitude | D'habitude, elle prenait le bus. |
| quand j'étais... | Quand j'étais enfant, je jouais dehors. |

**Passé composé — events, "what happened"**

| Signal | Example |
|---|---|
| hier | Hier, j'ai fini le rapport. |
| soudain | Soudain, la porte s'est ouverte. |
| d'abord... ensuite | D'abord, nous avons visité le musée, ensuite nous avons déjeuné. |
| enfin | Enfin, le train est arrivé. |
| une fois | Une fois, il a perdu ses clés. |

Honest caveat: the signals are strong hints, not laws — the real question is always how *you* are presenting the action. *Hier* with a state can still be imparfait (*Hier, il faisait beau* — the weather as background). Use the table to build the instinct, then let the film-versus-snapshot question make the final call.
Where do little words like me, te, nous go in a French sentence? I keep putting them after the verb like in English.

In French they go **before** the conjugated verb, in the slot between subject and verb:

- **Je te vois.** — I see you.
- **Tu me regardes.** — You're looking at me.
- **Elle nous écoute.** — She's listening to us.
- **Je vous attends.** — I'm waiting for you.
- **Il te téléphone demain.** — He'll phone you tomorrow.

English strands the pronoun after the verb ("I see *you*"), so your instinct keeps parking it at the end — in French that position doesn't exist for these words. Think of subject + pronoun + verb as a single block that travels together: *je te vois* is one unit.

They stay in that slot under negation too: **Je ne te vois pas.** (I don't see you.) The one big exception is affirmative commands — *Regarde-moi !* — which have their own record-worthy behavior.
How do I say "I see it" for a film, a letter, and some neighbors? Le, la, les confuse me.

The pronoun is a copy of the noun it replaces — same gender, same number:

- le film → **Je le vois.** (I see it.)
- la lettre → **Elle la lit.** (She's reading it.)
- les voisins → **Tu les connais ?** (Do you know them?)

And before a vowel sound, *le/la* shrink to *l'*: **Je l'ai vu hier** — "I saw it (the film) yesterday." You can't tell from *l'* alone whether it was *le* or *la*; context carries it.

One discipline point: the pronoun *replaces* the noun phrase entirely. You never say both — it's *je le vois*, never "je le vois le film". Once the pronoun steps in, the noun leaves the sentence.
Why is it "je lui parle" and not "je le parle" when I talk to my teacher?

Because *parler* connects to a person with **à**: *parler à quelqu'un*. And *à* + person is replaced by **lui** (to him / to her) or **leur** (to them):

- **Je parle à Marie. → Je lui parle.**
- **Je téléphone à mes parents. → Je leur téléphone.**
- **Elle répond au professeur. → Elle lui répond.**

Compare a verb that takes its person directly, with no *à*: *voir quelqu'un* → **Je le vois** (I see him). No *à*, so *le*, not *lui*.

The field test: build the full sentence with a name. If the name needs *à* in front of it (*je parle **à** Marie*), the pronoun is *lui/leur*. If the name slots in bare (*je vois Marie*), the pronoun is *le/la/les*. That one test sorts nearly every verb you'll meet.
Clinic: I wrote "Je le téléphone" for "I phone him" and "Je lui vois" for "I see her". Both wrong, apparently — what's the system?

Both are the same error in mirror image: you gave each verb the other one's pronoun.

- *Téléphoner* is an **à-verb** (*téléphoner à quelqu'un*) → **Je lui téléphone.** ✓
- *Voir* is a **direct verb** (*voir quelqu'un*) → **Je la vois.** (her) / **Je le vois.** (him) ✓

The system, sorted by verb family:

**Direct → le / la / les:** voir (je le vois), regarder (je la regarde), écouter (je les écoute), connaître, and — the one that surprises English speakers — *aider*: *aider quelqu'un* is direct, so "I help him" is **Je l'aide**, never *je lui aide*.

**À-verbs → lui / leur:** parler à, téléphoner à, répondre à, écrire à: **Je lui parle, je lui téléphone, je lui réponds, je lui écris.**

Run the name test whenever you're unsure: say the sentence with "Marie" in it. *Je téléphone à Marie* — there's the *à*, so *lui*. *Je vois Marie* — no *à*, so *le/la*.
What is the little word "y" doing in "J'y vais" and "On y va"?

*Y* replaces **à + a place** (and sometimes à + a thing). It's the French word for "there" when the place has already been mentioned:

- **Tu vas à Paris ? — Oui, j'y vais.** (Are you going to Paris? — Yes, I'm going [there].)
- **On y va !** — Let's go! (Literally "we go there" — the standard shout before leaving.)
- **Vous allez à la piscine ? — Nous y allons.** (We're going [there].)

It also serves with verbs built on *à* + thing: **Tu penses au projet ? — Oui, j'y pense.** (Are you thinking about the project? — Yes, I'm thinking about it.)

*Y* sits in the usual pronoun slot, before the verb. Your survival set is just three phrases: *j'y vais, on y va, j'y pense* — they cover a remarkable amount of daily French.
Au marché, la vendeuse demande : « Vous voulez des pommes ? » Je veux répondre « oui, deux kilos ». Mon amie dit que je dois utiliser « en ». Pourquoi ?

Votre amie a raison : il faut le mot **en**, qui remplace « de + nom » et garde la quantité.

La réponse complète est : « **Oui, j'en veux deux kilos.** »

Sans *en*, la phrase est incomplète : « je veux deux kilos » — deux kilos de quoi ? Le *en* porte les pommes dans la phrase, sans répéter le mot.

Le modèle est toujours le même — *en* se place avant le verbe, et la quantité reste après :
- **Tu as du pain ? — Oui, j'en ai.** (Tu en veux combien ? — J'en prends trois.)
- **Elle veut du café ? — Non, elle n'en veut pas.**

À retenir : en français, une quantité ne voyage jamais seule. On dit *j'en veux deux*, *j'en ai assez* (j'en ai assez = I've had enough of it), jamais « je veux deux » tout court quand le nom a disparu.
"Give it to me" — why is it "donne-le-moi" with the pronouns AFTER the verb, when you told me pronouns go before?

Because affirmative commands are the great exception. In an order, the pronouns move **after** the verb, chained with hyphens, and *me/te* put on their stronger forms *moi/toi*:

- **Donne-le-moi !** — Give it to me! (*le* = it, *moi* = to me)
- **Regarde-la !** — Look at her / look at it (the letter)!
- **Écoutez-les !** — Listen to them!
- **Donnez-moi le livre !** — Give me the book!

The order inside the chain is fixed: direct object first, then the person — *le/la/les* before *moi/toi/lui*: **Montre-le-lui !** (Show it to him!).

Why the exception exists, in one line: a command starts with the verb, so there's no subject slot for the pronouns to sit in — they trail behind instead. The moment the command turns negative, they march back to the front: *Ne me le donne pas !* — same words, normal order.
And the negative command? I wrote "Ne donne-le-moi pas" and it was corrected to something completely different.

The correction: **Ne me le donne pas.**

Negative commands cancel the exception. The pronouns leave their hyphenated trailer behind the verb and return to the normal statement slot, in the normal order, inside the *ne...pas* bracket:

- **Donne-le-moi !** → **Ne me le donne pas.** (Don't give it to me.)
- **Regarde-le !** → **Ne le regarde pas.** (Don't look at it.)
- **Écoute-moi !** → **Ne m'écoute pas.** (Don't listen to me.)

And the statement order they return to is worth fixing on its own, because it's the order you'll use everywhere else: *me/te/nous/vous* come **before** *le/la/les* — *je **te le** donne* (I'm giving it to you), *elle **me le** montre* (she shows it to me).

So the whole command system in one sentence: positive order — pronouns after, hyphenated, *moi/toi*; negative order — pronouns before, statement order, no hyphens.
In "Je vais le voir", why is "le" in the middle? I expected "je le vais voir" or "je vais voir le".

Because the pronoun belongs to the **infinitive**, not to the conjugated verb. *Le* means "him/it" as the object of *voir* (to see), so it parks directly in front of *voir*:

- **Je vais le voir.** — I'm going to see him/it.
- **Tu peux me téléphoner ?** — Can you phone me? (*me* belongs to *téléphoner*)
- **Elle veut les acheter.** — She wants to buy them. (*les* belongs to *acheter*)

The conjugated verbs here (*vais, peux, veut*) are just helpers — going to, can, wants to. The action that owns the pronoun is the infinitive, and French puts the pronoun immediately before the verb it belongs to.

Your two guesses are the two natural English-shaped errors: gluing the pronoun to the first verb (*je le vais voir*), or stranding it at the end (*je vais voir le*). The French rule is cleaner than both: pronoun directly before its own verb — conjugated or not.
Two pronouns at once: how do I say "I'm giving it to you" and "He gave it to me" in French?

The order in statements is fixed: **me / te / nous / vous come before le / la / les**.

- **Je te le donne.** — I'm giving it to you. (*te* = to you, *le* = it)
- **Elle nous les envoie.** — She sends them to us.

For "he gave it to me", both pronouns crowd in front of the auxiliary in the passé composé, and *le* elides before the vowel:

- **Il me l'a donné.** — He gave it to me. (*me* + *l'* + *a donné*)

One more of the same shape: **Tu me l'as dit.** — You told me (it).

There is a second rung to this ladder — *le/la/les* before *lui/leur*, as in *je le lui donne* ("I give it to him") — but meet it at recognition level for now. The *me/te + le* combination is the one daily French actually runs on: *je te le promets* (I promise you — literally "I promise it to you"), *tu me le montres ?* (will you show it to me?). Master this rung and two-pronoun sentences stop being scary.
How does French negation work? I wrote "Je sais ne pas" and got a bracket drawn around my verb.

Your teacher's bracket is the whole lesson: French negation is a **two-part frame** that wraps around the verb — *ne* before it, *pas* after it:

- **Je ne sais pas.** — I don't know.
- **Elle ne vient pas.** — She isn't coming.
- **Nous ne parlons pas anglais.** — We don't speak English.

Your *je sais ne pas* put the whole frame after the verb. In French the verb always sits *inside* the bracket.

Before a vowel, *ne* shrinks to *n'*: **Je n'ai pas le temps.** (I don't have time.) And the pronouns stay inside the frame too: **Je ne te vois pas.** (I don't see you.)

Picture *ne...pas* as two hands holding the verb — every negative sentence you build starts by placing those two hands.
In Paris I keep hearing "Je sais pas" and "T'inquiète pas" — where did the "ne" go? Should I copy that?

The *ne* didn't go anywhere mysterious — spoken French simply drops it, constantly. *Pas* ends up doing the negative work alone:

- **Je sais pas.** (= je ne sais pas — I don't know)
- **C'est pas grave.** (= ce n'est pas grave — it's no big deal)
- **T'inquiète pas.** (= ne t'inquiète pas — don't worry)

Two different skills follow from this. **Understanding it is essential**: if you listen for *ne* as your negative signal, you'll miss half the negatives spoken around you — listen for *pas* instead.

**Copying it is a register choice.** With friends, in relaxed conversation, dropping *ne* is normal and expected. In writing, exams, job interviews and careful speech, keep the full *ne...pas*. Dropping *ne* on paper isn't "informal style" — it's marked as an error. So: ears open, pen formal.
Why "Je n'ai pas de voiture" and not "pas une voiture"? When does de replace the article?

After a negative, the indefinite and partitive articles — *un, une, des, du, de la* — collapse into plain **de**:

- **Je n'ai pas de voiture.** — I don't have a car. (not *pas une voiture*)
- **Il n'y a pas de pain.** — There's no bread.
- **Nous n'avons pas d'enfants.** — We have no children.
- **Elle ne boit pas de café.** — She doesn't drink coffee.

The logic: the negative already says "zero of the thing", so the article that counts or portions it disappears, leaving bare *de*.

There is one famous exception: after **être**, the article stays:
- **Ce n'est pas un problème.** — That's not a problem.
- **Ce n'est pas une voiture, c'est une moto.** — That's not a car, it's a motorbike.

Rule of thumb: *de* after a negative everywhere — except with *être*, where *un/une/des* survive.
J'ai écrit « Je ne viens pas plus le mardi » pour dire que je ne viens plus le mardi. Ma prof a barré le « pas ». Pourquoi ?

Parce que **plus remplace pas** : la négation complète est *ne...plus*, et non *ne...pas plus*.

La phrase correcte : « **Je ne viens plus le mardi.** » (= je venais avant, mais c'est fini.)

C'est un système de remplacement — chaque mot négatif prend la place de *pas* dans la structure *ne...* :
- **ne...pas** — not : *Je ne sais pas.*
- **ne...plus** — not anymore, no more : *Elle ne fume plus.*
- **ne...jamais** — never : *Il ne téléphone jamais.*
- **ne...rien** — nothing : *Je ne vois rien.*

Attention à un détail : « je ne viens pas plus » existe en français, mais avec un autre sens — « je ne viens pas plus souvent que toi » (comparaison : pas davantage). Pour dire "not anymore", c'est *plus* seul, sans *pas*.
How do I say "I see nothing", "he says nothing", and answer "nothing" to "what are you doing?"

*Rien* (nothing) takes the *pas* seat in the negative frame:

- **Je ne vois rien.** — I see nothing / I don't see anything.
- **Il ne dit rien.** — He says nothing.
- **Elle ne mange rien.** — She eats nothing.

And as a one-word answer, *rien* stands alone:
- **Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? — Rien.** (What are you doing? — Nothing.)

Two bonus uses you'll meet immediately. *Rien* can be a subject, where it pulls *ne* after it: **Rien ne change.** (Nothing changes.) And the fixed phrase **de rien** — literally "of nothing" — is the standard reply to *merci*: "you're welcome, it's nothing."

English speakers must unlearn one reflex here: "I don't see nothing" is broken English, but *je ne vois rien* is perfect French — the two negative words are both required.
Someone asked me "Tu ne viens pas ?" and when I meant "yes I AM coming" my "oui" confused everyone. What's the right word?

The word is **si**. French has two yeses, and the second one exists precisely for this: contradicting a negative question or statement.

- **Tu ne viens pas ? — Si, je viens !** (Aren't you coming? — Yes, I AM coming!)
- **Tu viens ? — Oui, je viens.** (normal yes, after a positive question)

*Oui* after a negative question is genuinely ambiguous to French ears — it can sound like you're agreeing with the negative ("oui, c'est vrai, je ne viens pas"). *Si* removes all doubt: it means "on the contrary, yes".

Two companions from the same family:

- **Moi non plus.** — Me neither. (*Je ne viens pas. — Moi non plus.*)
- **Pas encore.** — Not yet. (*Tu as fini ? — Pas encore.*)

Learn *si* as a complete word with its own job, and negative questions stop being a trap.
Corrige mes phrases, s'il te plaît : « Je ne ai pas de chat. Elle ne vient pas plus à la piscine. Nous ne parlons pas l'italien très bien. »

Avec plaisir — il y a deux corrections sur trois phrases.

**1. « Je ne ai pas de chat » → « Je n'ai pas de chat. »**
Devant une voyelle, *ne* devient *n'* : je n'ai, tu n'as, il n'y a. On ne peut pas écrire « ne ai ».

**2. « Elle ne vient pas plus à la piscine » → « Elle ne vient plus à la piscine. »**
*Plus* remplace *pas* : la négation « not anymore » est *ne...plus*, sans *pas*.

**3. « Nous ne parlons pas l'italien très bien » — cette phrase est correcte !**
L'article défini (*l'italien*, comme *le français*) ne change pas après une négation. Seuls les articles indéfinis et partitifs (*un, une, des, du*) deviennent *de* : comparez « je n'ai pas **de** chat » (article indéfini → de) et « je ne parle pas **l'**italien » (article défini → il reste).

C'est exactement le genre de phrase qui semble fausse et ne l'est pas — bien vu de l'avoir incluse.
Give me the "there isn't any" patterns for a kitchen conversation — milk, bread, eggs, coffee.

The frame is *il n'y a pas de* + noun ("there is no / there isn't any"):

- **Il n'y a pas de lait.** — There's no milk.
- **Il n'y a pas d'œufs.** — There are no eggs. (*de* becomes *d'* before a vowel sound — *œufs* starts with one.)
- **Il n'y a plus de pain !** — There's no bread left! (*plus* = no more, when it ran out.)
- **Il n'y a jamais de café dans cette maison !** — There's never any coffee in this house! (*jamais* = never, for dramatic effect.)

Build notes: *il y a* (there is/are) negates to *il n'y a* — the *ne* slips in before the *y*. And the *de* is the negative-article rule at work: no *du lait* after a negative, just *de lait*.

The natural follow-up sentence brings the positive article back: **Il faut acheter du lait.** (We need to buy milk.)
Can French stack negatives? "He never says anything" and "I saw nobody" — in English those are double negatives and wrong.

French not only allows the stack — it requires it. Each negative word has its own slot, and they combine freely:

- **Il ne dit jamais rien.** — He never says anything. (*ne...jamais* wraps the verb; *rien* is the object.)
- **Je n'ai vu personne.** — I saw nobody. (In the passé composé, *personne* goes *after* the participle.)
- **Personne ne vient.** — Nobody comes. (*Personne* as subject, pulling *ne* behind it.)
- **Elle ne dit jamais rien à personne.** — She never says anything to anybody. (Three negative words, perfectly grammatical.)

The mental adjustment: English treats two negatives as canceling each other out, like arithmetic. French treats them as separate switches that each switch off one part of the sentence — time (*jamais*), thing (*rien*), person (*personne*). Once you think in switches rather than sums, the stack reads naturally.
Give me a reference table for French negative patterns — not, not anymore, never, nothing, nobody — with an example of each.

French negative patterns — each one replaces or extends *pas* in the frame *ne...* :

| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| ne...pas | not | Je ne sais pas. |
| ne...plus | not anymore, no more | Elle ne fume plus. |
| ne...jamais | never | Nous ne voyageons jamais en hiver. |
| ne...rien | nothing, not anything | Il ne dit rien. |
| ne...personne | nobody, not anybody | Je n'ai vu personne. |
| ne...pas encore | not yet | Le train n'est pas encore arrivé. |

Three notes for using the table. First, only *pas encore* keeps *pas* — every other pattern evicts it (*ne...plus*, never *ne...pas plus* for "not anymore"). Second, *personne* changes position in the passé composé: after the participle (*je n'ai vu personne*), while *rien* stays before it (*je n'ai rien vu*). Third, in spoken French the *ne* half of every row is routinely dropped — *je sais pas, elle fume plus* — but in writing the full frame is obligatory.
Comment poser une question simple en français, sans inversion compliquée ? Par exemple pour demander à un ami s'il vient demain.

La méthode la plus simple : gardez la phrase normale et **montez la voix à la fin**. La phrase déclarative devient une question par l'intonation :

- **Tu viens demain ?**
- **Vous avez l'heure ?**
- **C'est loin ?**

C'est la question de tous les jours — entre amis, dans la rue, au café. À l'écrit, on ajoute simplement le point d'interrogation.

Il existe une deuxième méthode, à peine plus formelle et tout aussi facile : commencez par **est-ce que**, sans changer l'ordre des mots :

- **Est-ce que tu viens demain ?**
- **Est-ce que vous avez l'heure ?**

Ces deux méthodes couvrent presque toutes les situations de la vie quotidienne. L'inversion (*Viens-tu demain ?*) existe, mais elle appartient surtout à l'écrit et aux situations formelles — vous n'en avez pas besoin pour être compris et poli à l'oral.
What does "est-ce que" actually do? It looks like it means "is it that".

Your literal reading is right — *est-ce que* is historically "is it that..." — but functionally it's just a **question switch**. Bolt it onto the front of any statement and the statement becomes a question, with the word order completely untouched:

- Tu viens. → **Est-ce que tu viens ?**
- Il fait froid. → **Est-ce qu'il fait froid ?** (*que* elides to *qu'* before a vowel)
- Vous avez l'heure. → **Est-ce que vous avez l'heure ?**

Register-wise it's the neutral middle of French: perfectly at home in speech and writing, with friends and with strangers. That's why learners are taught it first — it's the one form that is never wrong.

Compare the three gears of a French question: intonation (*Tu viens ?* — casual), *est-ce que* (neutral), inversion (*Viens-tu ?* — formal/written). *Est-ce que* is the gear you can stay in all day.
When do I flip the verb and pronoun, like "Parlez-vous français ?" or "As-tu le temps ?"

That's **inversion**: verb + hyphen + subject pronoun, flipped. It flavors a question formal, written, or ceremonially polite:

- **Parlez-vous français ?**
- **As-tu le temps ?**
- **Vient-elle demain ?**
- **Avez-vous une réservation ?**

At this level, invert only with **pronoun subjects** (je, tu, il, elle, nous, vous, ils, elles) — flipping a full noun phrase takes a different construction.

You'll meet inversion most often in frozen, everyday-formal phrases, and it's worth recognizing them as units: **Comment allez-vous ?** (How are you?), **Quelle heure est-il ?** (What time is it?), **Puis-je ?** (May I? — from *pouvoir*, whose je-form is the irregular *puis*).

In relaxed speech, French speakers mostly reach for intonation or *est-ce que* instead. Use inversion for writing, formal situations, and those set phrases — and recognize it everywhere.
Show me the same questions in all three French question forms side by side, with when I'd use each.

The same questions, three ways:

| Question | Intonation (casual speech) | Est-ce que (neutral) | Inversion (formal / written) |
|---|---|---|---|
| You're coming tomorrow? | Tu viens demain ? | Est-ce que tu viens demain ? | Viens-tu demain ? |
| Do you have a pen? | Tu as un stylo ? | Est-ce que tu as un stylo ? | As-tu un stylo ? |
| Do you speak French? | Vous parlez français ? | Est-ce que vous parlez français ? | Parlez-vous français ? |
| Is she ready? | Elle est prête ? | Est-ce qu'elle est prête ? | Est-elle prête ? |

How to choose: **intonation** is the sound of daily speech — friends, family, quick questions in shops. **Est-ce que** is the all-purpose middle: safe with everyone, in speech and in writing, never too casual and never stiff. **Inversion** belongs to formal writing, ceremonies, and set phrases (*Comment allez-vous ?*) — using it in a text message to a friend sounds like a legal document.

Notice that intonation and *est-ce que* leave the sentence order alone; only inversion rearranges anything. That's why learners live in the first two columns and visit the third.
Comment demander « où habites-tu ? » de trois façons différentes ? Et pour « quand » et « pourquoi » ?

Pour **où**, les trois méthodes :

1. Intonation (oral, familier) : « **Tu habites où ?** » — le mot interrogatif part à la fin de la phrase.
2. Est-ce que (neutre) : « **Où est-ce que tu habites ?** »
3. Inversion (formel, écrit) : « **Où habites-tu ?** »

Pour **quand**, même système :
- « **Tu pars quand ?** »
- « **Quand est-ce que tu pars ?** »
- « **Quand pars-tu ?** »

Pour **pourquoi**, une petite différence : il reste presque toujours **devant**, même à l'oral :
- « **Pourquoi est-ce que tu pars ?** »
- « **Pourquoi pars-tu ?** »

Les mots *où, quand, combien* peuvent finir une phrase parlée (« Ça coûte combien ? »), mais *pourquoi* et *comment* préfèrent le début de la phrase. C'est une habitude de la langue parlée, pas une règle absolue — mais en la suivant, vos questions sonneront naturelles.
Why can't I invert with a name — like "Est Paul venu ?" for "Has Paul come?" And what's the t doing in "va-t-il"?

Two good questions, both about how inversion is built.

**Names can't flip.** Inversion only works with the little pronoun subjects. With a noun subject, French does a two-step: the noun stays in front, and a matching pronoun flips after the verb as an echo:

- **Paul est-il venu ?** — literally "Paul, is-he come?" 

That's recognition-level machinery — in speech you'd simply say *Est-ce que Paul est venu ?* Your *Est Paul venu ?* tries to flip the whole noun phrase, which French grammar doesn't allow.

**The -t- is sound engineering.** When the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun starts with one, French welds in a buffer *t* so the two vowels don't collide:

- **Va-t-il au marché ?** (Is he going to the market?)
- **A-t-elle le temps ?** (Does she have time?)

In *est-il* or *vient-il*, by contrast, the *t* is part of the verb itself — nothing is inserted. But *va* and *a* have no *t* of their own, so one is supplied, hyphenated on both sides. Pure pronunciation, no meaning.
"Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?" and "Que fais-tu ?" — same question? And what is "qu'est-ce qui"?

Same question — "What are you doing?" — in two registers:

- **Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?** — the everyday form: *qu'est-ce que* + normal statement order. This is what people say.
- **Que fais-tu ?** — the formal/written form: *que* + inversion. This is what novels and formal letters say.

Now *qu'est-ce qui*: it asks about a **subject** — what thing is doing something — where *qu'est-ce que* asks about an object:

- **Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?** — What's happening? (What is going on?)
- **Qu'est-ce qui fait ce bruit ?** — What's making that noise?
- **Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?** — What are *you* doing? (you = subject, the doing = object)

The test: if your question can be rephrased "what is it that *does* X", it's *qu'est-ce qui*; if it's "what is it that [someone] does", it's *qu'est-ce que*. At the survival level, just fix the pair: *Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?* for "what's happening", *Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?* for "what are you up to".
Au café, je veux demander au serveur : est-ce qu'il a du thé, et combien coûte un café. Aide-moi à former les questions naturellement.

Bien sûr — voici les questions toutes prêtes, dans le registre juste pour un serveur (un inconnu, donc *vous*) :

Pour le thé : « **Pardon, est-ce que vous avez du thé ?** » — poli et neutre, parfait dans un café.

Pour le prix : « **Combien coûte un café, s'il vous plaît ?** » ou, plus simplement, en montrant la carte : « **Le café, c'est combien ?** »

Deux autres questions très utiles dans la même scène :
- « **Vous prenez la carte ?** » — Est-ce que vous acceptez les cartes bancaires ? (question par intonation, très naturelle au moment de payer)
- « **L'addition, s'il vous plaît.** » — Ce n'est même pas une question : c'est la phrase standard pour demander la note à la fin.

Remarquez le mélange naturel : *est-ce que* pour la première demande, l'intonation pour la question rapide au comptoir. C'est exactement comme ça que les Français parlent au café.
Job interview in French next week, and I also text my French friend daily. Which question forms where?

Match the form to the room — you have three gears:

**The interview (formal, spoken):** live in *est-ce que*. It's polished without being stiff: *Est-ce que l'équipe travaille le week-end ?*, *Est-ce que le poste demande des déplacements ?* Add inversion for the ceremonial set pieces: *Puis-je vous poser une question ?* (May I ask you a question?). Avoid bare intonation here — *Vous travaillez le week-end ?* to a future employer sounds like you're chatting in a bar.

**Formal writing (emails, cover letters):** inversion or *est-ce que*, both fine: *Pourriez-vous me confirmer l'heure ?* Never bare intonation on paper.

**Texting your friend (casual):** intonation rules, question words trailing: *Tu fais quoi ce soir ?*, *On se voit quand ?*, *T'as vu le match ?* Inversion here would sound like a notary drafted your text.

The good news: the middle gear, *est-ce que*, is acceptable literally everywhere. When nervous — say, in that interview — park yourself in it.
How do negative questions work? "Tu ne viens pas ?" — and how do I answer "yes" to it?

The negative simply rides inside whichever question form you choose:

- Intonation: **Tu ne viens pas ?**
- Est-ce que: **Est-ce que tu ne viens pas ?**
- Inversion (formal): **Ne viens-tu pas ?** — the *ne* moves in front of the flipped verb.

The answering system is the part English speakers must rewire. French has a dedicated yes for fighting a negative:

- **Tu ne viens pas ? — Si, je viens !** (Aren't you coming? — Yes I am!)
- **Tu ne viens pas ? — Non, je ne viens pas.** (No, I'm not.)

*Si* = "yes, contrary to what your question suggests"; *non* confirms the negative. Plain *oui* here is a muddle — avoid it.

One more formal variant you'll meet in writing: **N'as-tu pas faim ?** (Aren't you hungry?) — same *si/non* answers apply.

And a tone note: negative questions usually carry an expectation or mild surprise — *Tu ne viens pas ?!* is closer to "wait, you're NOT coming?!" than to a neutral information request. The neutral way to ask is the positive form.
Why is "les amis" pronounced like "lay-ZAH-mee"? Where does the Z come from?

That Z is the final *s* of *les*, waking up. It's called **liaison**.

On its own, the *s* of *les* is silent. But when the next word begins with a vowel, the consonant wakes up, pronounces as **z**, and glues the two words into one sound unit:

- **les‿amis** — "lay-ZAH-mee" (the friends)
- **les‿enfants** — "lay-ZAHN-fahn" (the children)
- **les‿hôtels** — "lay-ZOH-tel" (the hotels — the h is silent, so the vowel rule applies)

The same waking happens after *des, aux, mes, tes, ses* and other little words ending in a sleeping consonant. Before a consonant, everything sleeps as usual: **les livres** — no z, because *livres* starts with L.

French dislikes a hard chop between words; liaison is one of its glues. You'll never be marked wrong for *understanding* it — but producing it after *les/des* is obligatory, not decorative.
Pourquoi est-ce qu'on entend un son [z] dans « vous avez » et « nous avons », mais pas dans « vous parlez » ?

C'est la **liaison** : la consonne finale muette d'un mot se réveille devant une voyelle, et le *s* final se prononce [z].

- **vous‿avez** — le *s* de *vous* se réveille : [z]
- **nous‿avons** — même chose
- **ils‿ont**, **elles‿arrivent** — même chose

Devant une consonne, la lettre reste endormie : **vous parlez**, **nous mangeons** — aucun son [z], parce que *parlez* et *mangeons* commencent par une consonne.

Après les pronoms (*nous, vous, ils, elles*), la liaison est **obligatoire** : sans elle, la phrase sonne hachée et incorrecte. Vous la trouverez aussi après *les, des, aux* (les‿amis), après les nombres (**deux‿enfants**, **trois‿amis**) et dans des expressions figées comme **comment‿allez-vous**.

Règle pratique : si un petit mot se termine par une consonne muette et que le mot suivant commence par une voyelle, attendez-vous à entendre la liaison.
Is there any rule for which final letters are silent in French? It feels random.

It feels random, but there's a strong rule of thumb: **most final consonants are silent**.

- trop → "tro" (the p sleeps)
- grand → "grahn" (the d sleeps)
- froid → "frwa" (the d sleeps)
- petit → "puh-TEE" (the t sleeps)
- beaucoup → "boh-KOO" (the p sleeps)

The famous exception set is remembered by the English word **CaReFuL**: final **C, R, F, L** are *often* pronounced:

- sac → "sak" (C)
- mer → "mair" (R)
- neuf → "nuf" (F)
- sel → "sel" (L)

Two honest warnings. First, CaReFuL is a tendency, not a law — even it has traitors (the c of *tabac* is silent: "tah-BAH"). Second, a final written *-e* is never pronounced as its own syllable in standard French; it just marks that the consonant before it is awake (*grande* says its d because of the e).

So the working method: assume silence, pronounce C/R/F/L, and learn the famous rebels word by word. That covers the large majority of what you'll say.
What's the real difference between é and è? My app treats them as decoration.

They are two different sounds, and French ears hear them as clearly as English ears hear "ship" versus "sheep".

- **é** is a tight, closed "ay": **café** ("ka-FAY"), **été** (summer), **école** (school).
- **è** is an open, relaxed "eh": **mère** ("mair" — mother), **très** (very), **après** (after).

Say *café* with the open è sound and you've said a different, wrong word-shape; French listeners will notice instantly.

And accents in French are never decoration in spelling either — some of them change grammar and meaning outright: **a** (has) vs **à** (to/at): *il a un frère* / *il va à Paris*; **ou** (or) vs **où** (where). Dropping an accent in a text message is forgiven; in careful writing it's a spelling error like any other.

So: é and è tell your mouth which vowel to make, and the little hats and strokes elsewhere can change what the sentence means. Treat them as letters, not ornaments.
Why is it "l'homme" but "le héros"? Both start with h.

Because French *h* comes in two invisible flavors, and they behave completely differently.

**H muet** (mute h) acts as if it weren't there — the word effectively starts with a vowel, so elision and liaison happen normally:
- **l'homme** (the man), **l'hôtel**, **l'heure** (the hour)
- **les‿hommes** — with the z liaison: "lay-ZOM"

**H aspiré** (aspirated h) is never actually pronounced either — but it stands guard like a consonant and *blocks* elision and liaison:
- **le héros** (the hero), **la honte** (the shame), **le haricot** (the bean)
- **les héros** — no z link; a small silence separates the words.

There's no way to see the difference in spelling — both are written plain *h*. Dictionaries mark h aspiré words, and in practice you learn the common ones individually: *l'homme, l'hôtel, l'heure* on the mute side; *le héros, le haricot* on the aspiré side.

Recognition level is enough for now: if you hear *l'* or a z-liaison, the h was mute; if you hear *le/la* standing separate, it was aspiré.
French numbers after 60 make no sense to me. Why is 70 "soixante-dix" and 80 "quatre-vingts"?

Because standard French counts partly in **twenties** — a fossil of an older counting system:

- 70 = **soixante-dix** — literally "sixty-ten" (60 + 10)
- 71 = **soixante et onze** — "sixty and eleven"
- 80 = **quatre-vingts** — "four-twenties" (4 × 20), with an *s*
- 81 = **quatre-vingt-un** — the *s* drops when more follows
- 90 = **quatre-vingt-dix** — "four-twenty-ten" (80 + 10)
- 99 = **quatre-vingt-dix-neuf** — 80 + 19, the longest number name in the language

So 97 isn't a word you memorize; it's arithmetic you perform: *quatre-vingt-dix-sept*.

The honest regional footnote: Belgium says **septante** (70) and **nonante** (90) — but keeps *quatre-vingts* for 80. Much of Switzerland goes all the way: **septante, huitante, nonante**. Those forms are understood everywhere and are arguably more logical, but in France itself, use the *quatre-vingt* system — it's what every price, address and phone number will throw at you.
What are the nasal vowel sounds? "Bon" and "bonne" don't sound like the same word to me.

They aren't quite the same word — and you've heard one of French's signature effects.

French has **nasal vowels**: vowels pronounced with air escaping through the nose, where the written n or m is *not* pronounced as a consonant. There are four main ones:

- **un** — *un café* ("uhⁿ")
- **en / an** — *enfant, vent* ("ahⁿ")
- **on** — *bon, non* ("ohⁿ")
- **in** — *vin, matin* ("aⁿ" — like "eh" through the nose)

Now the magic: in **bon**, the n is absorbed into the nasal vowel — there is no "n" sound at all. Add the feminine *-e* and the n **wakes up** as a real consonant: **bonne** = "bon" with a clear n at the end. Same resurrection in *un/une* and *brun/brune*.

This is the same waking-consonant effect you meet in agreement (*grand/grande* wakes the d, *français/française* wakes the s). French spelling keeps consonants on the page even when asleep, because the feminine form — or a liaison — may need them awake.
Why does French chop words — j'aime, l'ami, d'accord, qu'il? Is it just laziness?

It's the opposite of laziness — it's a strict rule called **elision**. French avoids two vowel sounds colliding across a word boundary (a clash called hiatus), so when a little word ends in a vowel and the next word starts with one, the first vowel drops and an apostrophe takes its place:

- je aime → **j'aime**
- le ami → **l'ami**
- de accord → **d'accord**
- que il → **qu'il**
- la école → **l'école**
- ne a → **n'a** (il n'a pas)

The words that elide are a fixed, short list: *je, me, te, se, le, la, de, ne, que* — plus *si*, but only before *il/ils*: **s'il vous plaît**.

This is mandatory in writing, not casual slurring: *je aime* on paper is simply wrong, the way "a apple" is wrong in English (English solves the same collision by changing *a* to *an*). French solves it by amputation — neatly, and every time.
On m'a dit qu'il ne faut jamais faire la liaison après « et ». C'est vrai ? Et après un nom au singulier, comme « un étudiant intéressant » ?

Oui, pour « et », c'est vrai : **jamais de liaison après *et***. On dit « et elle » sans aucun son de liaison entre les deux mots — *et* ferme la porte.

Après un nom au singulier, la liaison est en général **absente** dans la langue courante : « un étudiant intéressant » se prononce sans liaison entre *étudiant* et *intéressant*. Elle existe dans un style très soutenu (discours officiel, lecture à voix haute), mais ne la cherchez pas : une liaison absente passe inaperçue, une liaison fausse s'entend immédiatement.

Les liaisons sûres, celles qu'il faut toujours faire :
- après *les, des, aux* : les‿amis, des‿enfants
- après les pronoms : nous‿avons, vous‿êtes, ils‿ont
- après les nombres : deux‿enfants, trois‿amis
- dans les expressions figées : comment‿allez-vous, de temps‿en temps

La règle de prudence : en cas de doute, pas de liaison vaut mieux qu'une liaison fausse.
Give me a pronunciation trap table — French words that don't sound like they look, with what to actually say.

Pronunciation traps — what you see vs what to say:

| Word | Looks like | Actually say | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| les amis | "less ah-mee" | "lay-ZAH-mee" | liaison: the s wakes as z |
| vous avez | "voo ah-vez" | "voo-ZAH-vay" | liaison after vous |
| l'homme | "luh hom" | "lom" | h is silent, one syllable |
| monsieur | "mon-see-ur" | "muh-SYUH" | completely irregular — learn as a sound |
| femme | "fem-meh" | "fam" | e pronounced "a" — a famous rebel |
| fils | "fills" | "feess" | means "son"; the l is silent, the s sounds |
| grand | "grand" | "grahn" | d silent, an is nasal |
| beaucoup | "bow-coup" | "boh-KOO" | final p silent |
| café | "ka-feh" | "ka-FAY" | é is a tight "ay" |
| très | "tress" | "treh" | è is an open "eh", s silent |

Two contrasts worth adding to your ear-training. **Fils** ("feess", son) versus **fil** ("feel", thread) — the spelling difference is one letter, the sound difference is total. And **monsieur** has a plural that changes again: *messieurs* ("may-SYUH"). French pronunciation is not random — it is regular rules plus a small museum of famous exceptions, and this table is most of the museum.
Walk me through buying bread at a Paris bakery — what will they say, what do I say?

Here's the whole scene, with your lines ready to use:

**Vous :** *Bonjour Madame, je voudrais une baguette, s'il vous plaît.*
(Good morning, I'd like a baguette, please.)

**La boulangère :** *Bien sûr. Ce sera tout ?*
(Of course. Will that be all?)

**Vous :** *Oui, merci. Ça fait combien ?*
(Yes, thanks. How much does that come to?)

**La boulangère :** *Un euro vingt.*
(One euro twenty.)

**Vous :** *Voilà. Merci, bonne journée !*
(Here you are. Thanks, have a good day!)

Three notes. First, *je voudrais* ("I would like") is the polite workhorse — *je veux* ("I want") sounds like a demand. Second, *ce sera tout ?* is a fixed question; the answer for "yes, that's all" is *Oui, ce sera tout.* Third, the whole exchange runs on *vous* — a bakery is vous territory, and your *s'il vous plaît* matches it. Open with *bonjour* before anything else: in France the greeting isn't decoration, it's the door.
Bonjour ! Je suis dans un café à Paris. Je voudrais commander, mais je ne sais pas quoi dire au serveur. On joue la scène ?

Avec plaisir — je joue le serveur, et je vous guide en même temps.

D'abord, les phrases dont vous avez besoin :
- « **Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.** » — la formule de base, polie et parfaite.
- Un *café*, à Paris, c'est un expresso. Si vous le voulez plus long : « **un café allongé** ». Avec du lait : « **un café crème** ».
- Pour accompagner : « **et un croissant** ».

Je commence la scène. Le serveur arrive et dit :

« **Bonjour, bienvenue ! Vous désirez ?** »

À vous de répondre, en français, avec « Je voudrais... ». N'ayez pas peur des erreurs : je corrige doucement, comme un serveur patient, et la scène continue. On commande d'abord la boisson.
The café asked me "Sur place ou à emporter ?" and the board says "menu" but I just wanted a sandwich. Decode both.

Two separate traps, both very French.

**Sur place ou à emporter ?** = "For here or to go?" *Sur place* means eating in, at a table; *à emporter* means takeaway. Your answer: **Sur place, s'il vous plaît.** (In some cafés the price even differs — eating in can cost a little more.)

**Le menu** is the bigger trap: on a French board, *le menu* is not the list of dishes — it's the **set meal**, a fixed-price combination (starter + main, or main + dessert). The list itself is **la carte**. If you order "le menu", you've committed to the formula of the day. To browse before deciding, ask: **La carte, s'il vous plaît.**

Related word on the same board: **la formule** — a deal bundle (sandwich + drink + dessert, for example). So your sandwich, decoded: point at the sandwich, say *sur place* or *à emporter*, and only say *le menu* or *la formule* when you actually want the bundle.
How do I ask for and follow simple directions in French? I get lost after "à gauche".

The asking part is one fixed sentence:

**Pardon, Madame — la gare, c'est loin d'ici ?**
(Excuse me — is the station far from here?)

And here is a typical answer, decoded piece by piece:

**Non, c'est tout près. Allez tout droit, puis tournez à gauche au feu, et c'est sur votre droite.**
(No, it's very close. Go straight ahead, then turn left at the traffic light, and it's on your right.)

Your anchor vocabulary:
- **tout droit** — straight ahead
- **à gauche / à droite** — left / right
- **tournez** — turn (vous form, because strangers)
- **prenez la première rue** — take the first street
- **au coin** — at the corner
- **c'est à cinq minutes** — it's five minutes away
